s: Part four.
Enforcement and handoffs.
This is task statement one point four: implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns.
By the end of this part, you'll know the three rungs of the enforcement ladder, what a handoff record must carry, and how a handoff to a human differs from one between stages.
Let's start with a picture.
A sign in a staff kitchen asking people to wash up is a request.
A barrier that won't open until you tap a card is a guarantee.
Both express the same wish.
Only one of them holds on the day somebody is in a hurry.
Instructions in a prompt are the sign.
Most of the time they work.
And that's exactly the trap.
A rule that holds nineteen times out of twenty looks like a rule.
Right up until the twentieth run writes to something that matters.
If a step must happen, something outside the model's judgment has to check that it happened.
Every time.
The technical principle.
Hold on to this line.
A prompt is a request, and code is a guarantee.
If a step must happen, encode it as a gate your code evaluates.
Not as a sentence competing with everything else in the context window.
And there's an order in which you reach for enforcement.
It's called the enforcement ladder.
Three rungs.
First.
Structural.
Withhold the tool.
A stage that must not write has no write tool in its tools list.
Second.
Deterministic interception.
A PreToolUse hook that denies the call outright.
No amount of model reasoning can route around it.
Third.
Contractual.
A handoff record the next stage validates before it does anything.
So an out-of-order or incomplete stage fails loudly, at the boundary.
The price is the same in all three.
You give up some flexibility.
And every gate is code someone has to maintain.
Question one.
A prerequisite gate.
Here's the scenario.
An account-security agent can call verify_identity and reset_password.
Despite clear system prompt instructions, audit logs show about one reset in two hundred happening before identity was verified.
Compliance requires zero exceptions.
And when a reset is blocked, the agent should explain why and escalate, rather than retry.
What's the answer?
Take a second.
A bank teller's cash drawer stays locked until the ID scanner turns green.
The teller can't hand over money first and check ID later, however long the queue.
If the scanner refuses, a message tells the teller to call a supervisor.
The answer.
A PreToolUse hook that tracks session state, and denies reset_password until verify_identity has succeeded.
It runs in code, before the call executes.
So the model can't bypass it.
And the denial carries a permissionDecisionReason.
For example: "Identity not verified.
Do not retry.
Escalate."
That reason gives the model the context to escalate, instead of retrying with different parameters.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a PostToolUse hook that flags unverified resets for review.
Why?
PostToolUse runs after the tool has already executed.
So the reset has already happened.
It detects.
It does not prevent.
Wrong: move the rule into CLAUDE.md.
Why?
That helps a rule persist.
But it's still advisory.
And most of the time is not zero exceptions.
Wrong: add few-shot examples showing verification first.
Why?
Examples improve consistency, not compliance.
The constraint words that decide it are "zero exceptions" and "explain and escalate rather than retry."
Hold on to this line.
If one step must come before another every time, block the second step in code until the first has succeeded.
And say why.
Now the contrast between keeping a rule in view, and enforcing it.
Question two.
This one is pick two.
Here's the scenario.
A long-running Claude Code job in continuous integration migrates a large codebase.
The opening prompt says never edit files under db/migrations/applied/.
The conversation compacts twice.
And afterwards, the agent edits an applied migration.
The team wants the rule enforced every time.
And still visible to the model after compaction, so it plans around the rule.
Which two?
Take a second.
A door has a "staff only" sign, and a lock.
The sign tells people where not to go, so they can plan their route.
The lock makes the rule hold on the day someone forgets.
And a sign that falls off the wall halfway through the day protects nothing.
In exam terms, compaction is when a long conversation gets summarised to free up room.
And instructions in an opening prompt can be dropped when that happens.
The answers.
First.
A PreToolUse hook matched to Edit and Write, that denies any path under the applied migrations folder, with a reason.
Second.
Move the rule into the project CLAUDE.md.
It's re-injected into context on every request, so it survives compaction.
The hook is enforcement.
CLAUDE.md is persistence.
They're separate jobs.
Without CLAUDE.md, the model keeps colliding with the hook.
Without the hook, the rule is still only advisory.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: repeat the rule three times in the opening prompt.
Why?
That changes the odds, not the guarantee.
Wrong: raise the compaction trigger, so the prompt is summarised later.
Why?
The failure becomes rarer.
Nothing is enforced.
Wrong: mark the files with readOnlyHint.
Why?
A tool scheduling hint is not a file permission.
Question three.
The notes add a sibling.
Here's the scenario.
A normalise, validate, load workflow.
The prompt says load must never run unless validate passed.
The conversation compacted twice.
And the agent went straight from normalise to load.
What are the real enforcements?
Take a second.
The answer.
There are two.
First.
A load-stage subagent whose tools list contains no write tool, until it receives a validated handoff.
Second.
A PreToolUse hook that denies the load tool when the validation artifact is missing.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: reposition the prompt text.
Wrong: raise maxTurns.
Why are both wrong?
The agent didn't run out of room.
It skipped a step.
So when do you use a prompt instruction, when CLAUDE.md, and when a hook?
A prompt instruction.
For guidance that's fine to follow most of the time.
CLAUDE.md.
For rules that must stay visible across a long session.
A hook, or a withheld tool.
For anything that must hold every time.
The configuration chapter goes deeper on what belongs in CLAUDE.md, versus rules files and skills.
Hold on to this line.
CLAUDE.md keeps the rule in view.
The hook makes it true.
Now handoff records between stages.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A two-stage pipeline extracts claims data to a staging file, then loads it into a warehouse.
The load stage starts whenever a handoff file exists in the run folder.
After a crash and rerun, the loader picked up a handoff left by the earlier aborted run.
And it loaded a stale, half-validated dataset.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
A warehouse accepts a delivery only if the paperwork matches today's order number, and the seal on the box is unbroken.
A box left on the dock from last week's cancelled order is refused.
Even though it looks like a delivery.
The answer.
In exam terms, a handoff record makes a stage boundary real only if the next stage validates it before acting.
So the loader runs four checks.
One.
It checks the run_id.
Two.
It checks that stage next_expected names the load stage.
Three.
It checks that the gate status is pass, and was evaluated by code.
Four.
It checks the artifact's checksum.
Any mismatch is a refusal.
And that refusal is the enforcement.
Everything else is a suggestion.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: have the extraction stage write a more detailed prose summary.
Why?
Prose asserts a result without evidence.
And a clearer claim from the old run is still a claim from the old run.
Wrong: include the whole dataset inline in the handoff.
Why?
Handoffs carry addresses, not payloads.
Inlining bloats every downstream context.
And it still doesn't identify the run.
Wrong: have the load agent message the extraction agent to confirm.
Why?
That's another probabilistic claim.
And in a hub-and-spoke design, workers don't talk directly.
So what goes in a handoff record?
The notes list the fields.
Let's take them one at a time.
A handoff_version.
A run_id.
A stage section, with completed, next_expected, and a timestamp.
A gate section.
It holds the status.
The individual checks, with their expected and observed values. evaluated_by, set to code.
And a pointer to the evidence.
A produced section.
It holds the artifact's address, a row count, and a sha256 checksum.
A decisions_locked list.
An open_questions list.
And a budget section, with dollars spent, dollars remaining, and turns used.
Why the budget?
So a late stage knows its runway, instead of discovering the cap by hitting it.
Question five.
The notes include one that isolates a single field.
Here's the scenario.
An extraction stage writes a nine hundred megabyte file.
It hands over a paragraph saying extraction completed, the row count looked reasonable, and validation passed.
What's the primary defect?
Take a second.
The answer.
The handoff mixes up a model's claim with a verified result.
A model saying "validation passed" is a claim.
A program comparing forty-two observed columns against forty-two expected is evidence.
That's what evaluated_by code distinguishes.
And only evidence should open a gate.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: inline the data.
Why?
That's backwards.
Wrong: switch prose to JSON.
Why?
It doesn't help if it still only asserts.
Wrong: add the session id, so the load can resume extraction.
Why?
That confuses recovery with handoff.
Hold on to this line.
The next stage's first act is to check the paperwork.
And it refuses on any mismatch.
Next, locked decisions.
Question six.
Here's the scenario.
A multi-stage financial extraction pipeline hands work between subagents.
Stage one agreed with the client to store all amounts in minor units, meaning cents.
And all dates in UTC.
Stage three, running later from its own work order, stored amounts in major units.
Reconciled totals were off by a factor of one hundred.
The handoff carries only artifact paths.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
A wedding planner agrees with the couple that every price is quoted in euros.
The caterer, briefed separately, quotes in pounds.
And the budget sheet falls apart.
Writing "all prices in euros, already agreed" on every supplier brief would have prevented it.
The answer.
Add a decisions_locked field to the handoff record.
The next stage reads it, and must not relitigate it.
Settled decisions have to travel with the work.
Or the next stage rediscovers them differently.
The notes call that the most expensive form of subagent drift.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: pass stage one's full conversation history to stage three.
Why?
That defeats context isolation.
It bloats the window.
And the decision still has to be dug out of prose.
Wrong: a prompt line telling stage three to stay consistent with whatever earlier stages decided.
Why?
It points at information stage three was never given.
Wrong: a larger model, to infer the convention.
Why?
No model can reliably infer a convention the data doesn't state.
Hold on to this line.
Decisions that are settled go in the handoff, in writing.
So no later stage can reopen them.
Now the handoff to a human.
That's a different kind of record.
Question seven.
Here's the scenario.
When the refund agent escalates, it writes a friendly paragraph to the human queue.
Human agents open the full conversation transcript for almost every ticket.
They're looking for the order, what was tried, and why it failed.
Handling time doubles.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
A nurse ending a shift doesn't hand over a recording of the whole day.
They give a short chart.
Patient.
Problem.
What was tried.
What to watch.
What to do next.
The next nurse can act in two minutes, instead of forty.
The answer.
A structured handoff, with fields.
Let's list them.
The customer id.
The issue type.
The root cause.
What was attempted.
The escalation reason, meaning the specific policy that required it.
The amount.
And a recommended next action.
The person acting on it should never need the transcript.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: attach the full transcript.
Why?
That formalises the problem.
Wrong: write a longer, more detailed paragraph.
Why?
It's slower to scan.
And it still buries the fields.
Wrong: let human agents resume the agent's session to question it.
Why?
Session resume restores a conversation for an agent, not a decision summary for a person.
And it adds another round trip.
So, the contrast.
A stage-to-stage handoff record is for a machine.
It carries addresses, gate evidence, locked decisions and budget.
And the next stage validates it.
A human handoff summary is for a person.
It carries the decision inputs in plain fields, so they can act without reading the history.
Both refuse to make the reader dig through a transcript.
One last mechanic from the notes.
For runs that coordinate dozens to hundreds of agents, turn-by-turn delegation stops being the right shape.
The documentation points to the Workflow tool.
It moves the orchestration into a script the runtime runs outside the conversation.
It needs the TypeScript Agent SDK at version zero point three point one hundred forty-nine or later.
And Workflow must be in allowedTools.
Treat it as the escape hatch for scale.
Not the default.
That's part four.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
A prompt is a request, and code is a guarantee.
Climb the ladder: from withholding the tool, to denying it in a hook, to a handoff record the next stage validates.
Put locked decisions in the record.
And give humans a structured summary, not a transcript.
